Dear Secretary Reese:

        The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), through this filing,1
submits proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve
Markets Tariff (“Tariff”),2 to establish a Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement
(“ZGIA”),3 associated study process and operational requirements, and market and resource
adequacy rules to accommodate Zero-Injection Generation Resources (“ZG Resource”) that intend
to serve load interconnecting at the same substation as the Generating Facility. The ZGIA proposal
will help streamline the MISO generator interconnection process by providing expedited review
of the addition of ZG Resources that have little or no impact on the Transmission System because
they are limited to serving load at the same substation and voltage level.

        The ZGIA proposal is responsive to certain of the concerns raised by the Commission in
the Order Instituting Proceeding Under FPA Section 206 4 in Docket No. EL26-70-000 (“Show
Cause Order” or “SCO”) by proposing a permanent solution for generation resources that provides:
(i) an interconnection service framework for generation supporting load at the same substation,

including co-located load; (ii) a defined interconnection study processes tailored to zero-injection
configurations, including co-location arrangements; (iii) potential reductions in Network Upgrade
requirements where a more limited form of Interconnection Service is all that is needed, and (iv)
clear allocation of operational and planning responsibilities. Specifically, this filing responds to
the Commission’s concerns by presenting a set of just and reasonable Tariff revisions setting forth
the generator interconnection study process and generator interconnection service applicable to
generation serving co-located load. However, MISO notes that this filing is not intended to address
all issues raised in the Show Cause Order.

        As acknowledged in the Show Cause Order, MISO began development of ZG
Interconnection Service and the ZGIA through its stakeholder process months prior to the issuance
of the Show Cause Order. While MISO has adapted elements of its proposed process to better
comply with the requirements of the Show Cause Order, this filing addresses a specific need within
the MISO region, adapting existing and proven processes to provide a valuable tool to address co-
location concerns, including many of those raised in the Show Cause Order. MISO therefore
submits that the proposed ZG Interconnection Service construct is just, reasonable, and useful in
the MISO region independent of its responsiveness to the Show Cause Order. Other issues raised
in the Show Cause Order, including the appropriate transmission service for large and co-located
loads and the treatment of generation serving electrically proximate large loads, will be addressed
through MISO’s forthcoming large load proposals.

        MISO requests that the Tariff revisions submitted herewith be made effective October 18,
2026, which is more than sixty (60) days—and less than one hundred twenty (120) days—from
the date of this submission. As discussed below and in the supporting testimony of Mr. Keyser,5
action is needed in the near term to address the reliability impacts and resource adequacy needs
associated with the impending interconnection of Load, including the anticipated interconnection
of significant large loads.

    I.    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

          A.       Background

       The United States is in the midst of an unprecedented energy transition. Large load
customers, including artificial intelligence (“AI”) data centers and next-generation manufacturing
technologies, are driving a surge in interconnection requests. This growth is driven primarily by
data center investment.6 As observed by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation
(“NERC”), the largest contributor to this accelerated demand growth is data center additions with

18 GW of data center loads projected by 2035.7 The MISO region is no exception to this energy
transition. Energy-intensive loads such as data centers, manufacturing expansion, and
electrification are adding sustained, concentrated load at levels not seen in decades.8 While
electricity demand growth has been relatively flat with an annual average of just 0.5% between
2009 and 2024, MISO is projecting a substantial increase of 1% to 2% per year through 2044, with
even higher growth rates in the near term.9

       This growth has understandably drawn the focus of Relevant Electric Retail Rate
Authorities (“RERRA”), stakeholders and federal policymakers. On January 23, 2025, President
Trump issued an Executive Order stating, “[i]t is the policy of the United States to sustain and
enhance America’s global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic
competitiveness, and national security.”10 On July 23, 2025, an Executive Order titled
“Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure,” the Trump Administration
announced its intention to pursue bold, large-scale industrial plans to incentivize critical
manufacturing and data center development:

                  We will pursue bold, large-scale industrial plans to vault the United
                  States further into the lead on critical manufacturing processes and
                  technologies that are essential to national security, economic
                  prosperity, and scientific leadership. These plans include artificial
                  intelligence (AI) data centers and infrastructure that powers them,
                  including high-voltage transmission lines and other equipment. It
                  will be a priority of my Administration to facilitate the rapid and
                  efficient buildout of this infrastructure by easing Federal regulatory
                  burdens.11

       On October 23, 2025, the Secretary of Energy directed the Commission to consider an
Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”) focused on the timely and orderly
interconnection of large loads to the interstate transmission system.12 The Secretary’s

correspondence to the Commission in support of the ANOPR emphasized the importance of the
timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory integration of large loads:

                   To usher in a new era of American prosperity, we must ensure all
                   Americans and domestic industries have access to affordable,
                   reliable, and secure electricity. To do this, large loads, including AI
                   data centers, served by public utilities must be able to connect to the
                   transmission system in a timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory
                   manner. This is an urgent issue that requires prompt attention.13

        On June 18, 2026, the Commission issued the Show Cause Order.14 The Show Cause Order
recognizes the unprecedented increase in requests for transmission service to serve large loads
along with the growing interest in co-location arrangements to serve those large loads.15 The Show
Cause Order cites a lack of clarity and consistency in Regional Transmission Organizations’ or
Independent System Operators’ tariffs regarding the rates, terms, and conditions of service that
apply to flexible large loads, co-location arrangements, load with behind the meter generation, and
generating facilities with electrically proximate large load or co-located load.16 Ultimately, the
Show Cause Order requires MISO to show cause as to why the Tariff remains just and reasonable
without provisions addressing certain large load and co-location issues or, in the alternative,
explain what changes to the Tariff would remedy the Commission’s concerns.17

           B.      Addressing the Influx of Large Loads in the MISO Region

        The MISO region is experiencing a significant influx of large load additions—primarily
from data centers, cryptocurrency miners, and other processes that require larger load
interconnections. Large load growth presents a unique challenge because MISO must balance
multiple objectives simultaneously. MISO seeks to facilitate economic development and timely,
cost-effective access to the Transmission System while maintaining reliability and operational
integrity.

        MISO, its member states, and stakeholders are developing multiple initiatives to address
evolving system conditions and to support efficient interconnection prior to and after the issuance
of the Show Cause Order. In recognition of urgent needs to address large load and co-located load
growth, MISO established a temporary, targeted Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”)
process to accelerate the generator interconnection process limited to generators necessary to serve
certain critical, near-term load additions.

        In addition, MISO improved the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan’s (“MTEP”)
Expedited Project Review (“EPR”) process to quickly study Network Upgrades needed to support
large loads. MISO also initiated the MISO-SPP Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue Study
(“JTIQ”) which aims at building transmission network upgrades along the MISO-SPP seams to
enable large amounts of new generation. While these initiatives provide important benefits, they
neither fully address the reliability and operational challenges associated with accelerating large
load growth, nor do they address all concerns raised in the Show Cause Order. Accordingly, MISO
recognizes that additional Tariff-based solutions are necessary to establish clear reliability
expectations, improve operational visibility, and facilitate timely integration of large loads in a
manner that is both reliable and non-discriminatory. These solutions must also consider and
address the unique planning and operational characteristics of large load interconnection customers
and hyperscale data centers, in particular. The ZGIA is one of these forthcoming solutions.

        MISO’s ZGIA proposal is well aligned with the Commission’s goals and objectives of
transparency, affordability and reliability. This proposal is one element in MISO’s response to the
Commission’s desire for prompt action to address the rapid growth of large loads, related
interconnection requests, and a surge in interest in co-located generation. The Show Cause Order
addresses the unprecedented increase in requests for transmission service to serve large load, as
well as the growing interest in the co-location of loads with generation facilities (i.e., co-location
arrangements), while acknowledging the challenges associated with providing the transmission
service necessary to reliably serve the ongoing influx of large loads.18 The Show Cause Order
states that MISO has not yet proposed Tariff revisions to address the challenges associated with
the integration of large and co-located loads.19 The Show Cause Order requires MISO to show
cause as to how its Tariff remains just and reasonable, or to explain what changes would remedy
the Commission’s concerns.20

        MISO is moving quickly on proposals that had been previously incorporated into the Large
Load Working Group (“LLWG”) workplan and is also engaging with stakeholders, including the
Organization of MISO States, Inc. (“OMS”), in an expedited manner to develop the broader set of
solutions outlined in the August 3, 2026, motion filed by MISO and the MISO Transmission
Owners to hold all proceedings related to the Show Cause Order in abeyance for 90 days.21 The
Abeyance Motion explained that MISO and the MISO Transmission Owners required additional
time to continue the stakeholder process and submit FPA section 20522 filings that address the

       The Abeyance Motion emphasized that MISO, in collaboration with stakeholders and the
OMS, has been working to identify and implement solutions to facilitate speed to reliable power.25
These efforts include two already-implemented initiatives: (1) the one-time, targeted ERAS
process to accelerate generator interconnection for near-term resource adequacy needs; and (2)
improving the MTEP EPR process to enable the rapid study and approval of transmission upgrades
necessary for the addition of large loads.26 MISO explained that it also created the LLWG to
provide a dedicated and consolidated stakeholder forum for prioritizing and focusing efforts to
both identify critical issues and develop corresponding solutions to integrate large loads reliably
and cost effectively.27

       MISO has developed a prioritized work plan to accelerate consideration of the challenges
presented by large load growth in the MISO region through its stakeholder process.28 This process
has resulted in the development of groups of potential solutions and improvements to various
MISO processes, which MISO intends to submit for Commission review in a series of filings.29
The present filing represents the first of this series.

           C.     The ZGIA Proposal Supports Co-Location and Provides Speed to Power

         Co-location has been widely recognized as one of the most valuable tools in achieving
“speed to power” in a reliable and efficient manner and MISO’s ZGIA co-location solution has
been prioritized within the LLWG’s efforts. The ZGIA and related study process proposed in this
filing is the first of the proposed solutions to come from the LLWG. The ZGIA construct is the
product of significant effort by MISO, the OMS, and stakeholders that began prior to the Show
Cause Order and was refined in response to the Show Cause Order. The ZGIA framework will
address not only large load interconnections and co-located generation but it also will help
streamline the interconnection process for Interconnection Customers serving co-located load.30

Hence, the ZGIA proposal serves two important purposes. First, the ZGIA framework addresses
several of the Commission’s concerns raised in the Show Cause Order. Second, the ZGIA
framework addresses improvements to the interconnection process in addition to the Commission's
stated concerns, such that it will have independent benefits for all interconnection customers.

         MISO explored several potential scopes for its ZG Interconnection Service product through
the stakeholder process including limiting it to load and generation connecting to the Transmission
System behind the same Point of Interconnection and expanding it to encompass load located
“proximate” to generation. After extensive consideration, MISO determined that limiting ZG
Interconnection Service to load and generation behind the same Point of Interconnection is too
strict an approach for the MISO Transmission System as it would exclude configuration options
that MISO is aware that developers are considering for adjacent load and generation where
injections to the broader Transmission System can be effectively limited and monitored.
Following further discussion and evaluation with stakeholders, MISO also determined that
expanding the ZGIA and ZG Interconnection Service construct to accommodate “electrically
proximate” load and generation would have raised novel reliability and transmission service
challenges that would not be easily resolved in a timely manner for the unique processes that
underpin MISO’s transmission and interconnection services. In addition, stakeholders raised
concerns that extending the proposal to serving proximate load beyond the same substation could
result in the potential for retail wheeling and conflict with retail regulatory constructs. Rather than
delay a significant and important tool to support co-location, MISO chose not to incorporate a
“proximate” load solution in this initial filing.31 Accordingly, this filing is limited to addressing
generation and load at the same substation and does not attempt to resolve the separate issues
presented by generation serving electrically proximate large load. MISO’s forthcoming Load
Addition Resource Study (“LARS”) process is intended to address those issues by providing a
coordinated study framework for load additions and associated new generation that are electrically
proximate but do not satisfy the ZGIA’s narrower requirements.

         This filing proposes Tariff revisions to establish the ZGIA construct as a Tariff-defined
process to take advantage of the benefits of co-location of generation and load. The ZGIA
framework creates a path for a planned generator that will connect at the same substation and
voltage level as existing or proposed load (including large loads) to interconnect quickly, with
strict limitations on injections further onto the Transmission System, which and correspondingly
reduce potential for Transmission System Impacts and expensive Network Upgrade. Load
customers, including large load customers, will benefit from ZGIA interconnection studies that
recognize on-site generation, potentially reducing network upgrade requirements to interconnect.
As discussed in more detail below, the proposed ZGIA framework includes a new load at the same
substation and voltage level as a generation resource. The figure below depicts load taking firm-

of electrically proximate load and generation, LARS, will further address the Commission’s

        The ZGIA proposal represents another critical tool to help support the timely, reliable, cost-
effective integration of new large loads into the MISO system. It efficiently leverages existing
MISO processes and practices to serve as a robust incremental solution. MISO notes that this is
one of several upcoming Tariff solutions that will be filed with the Commission to collectively
address the issues raised in the Show Cause Order. MISO appreciates the guidance and direction
provided in the Show Cause Order and is committed to continuing its collaborative efforts with
the states and stakeholders to deliver additional tools to meet the unique challenges associated with
integrating large loads.

         D.      Anticipated Complementary Solutions

        MISO has been advancing a coordinated set of solutions designed to balance speed to
power, fairness, and, most importantly, reliability. In particular, MISO has developed two solutions
that are responsive to the Commission’s concerns noted in the Show Cause Order surrounding the
interconnection and study processes for co-location arrangements and service of proximate large
loads.

        The ZGIA proposal identified in this filing is the product of a stakeholder process that
began prior to the Show Cause Order to address not only large load interconnection and co-location
issues, but also improvements to the interconnection process in general. By formalizing the ZGIA
construct in the Tariff,35 MISO can provide a limited, structured option to support large load
integration, co-location, and refinements to the interconnection process through:

                   load;
              •    Defined interconnection study processes tailored to zero-injection configurations;
              •    Potentially reduced network upgrade requirements where appropriate; and
              •    Clear allocation of operational and planning responsibilities.

        This construct enables a pathway for certain large load configurations to achieve speed to
reliable power while maintaining system reliability.

        The ZGIA framework represents an initial step in a broader set of solutions to address the
concerns expressed in the Show Cause Order and to meet the evolving needs of the MISO region.
These ongoing efforts reflect the iterative nature of MISO’s response to rapidly changing load
conditions and the need for continued stakeholder collaboration. To that end, as noted above,
MISO will be submitting additional proposals to further address large load integration as discussed
in the Abeyance Motion.

        In addition to the ZGIA proposal submitted herein, MISO is also developing through the
stakeholder process at the LLWG its Load Addition and Resource Study process. LARS will assess
the transmission infrastructure needed to meet new large loads and new generation in an efficient
process that can be executed on a shorter timeline, further supplementing the opportunities
available for members to facilitate new large spot loads effectively. This process is expected to
position MISO and its members to ensure resource adequacy and protect customers from
unnecessary investments relating to spot large load siting.

        More specifically, LARS will analyze generation and transmission using the same study
assumptions applied in the standard generator interconnection process and MISO’s MTEP. The
studies will be run in parallel, and will finish at approximately the same time—within 120 days—
with the load/transmission model incorporating both the planned generation and planned load.36
LARS, as currently conceived, will address similar issues to those the Show Cause Order identified
related to interconnection customers serving electrically proximate large load or co-located load.37
Thus, while the instant ZGIA filing addresses the generator interconnection service and study
framework for generation serving ZG Associated Load, LARS will address the distinct study issues
presented by new generation and large load that are electrically proximate but are not eligible for
ZG Interconnection Service. It is important to note that neither the ZGIA construct nor LARS
proposal include new transmission service products specific to serving co-located or proximate
load or address flexible large loads willing to limit transmission service. Transmission service

 II.     OVERVIEW OF ZGIA PROPOSAL AND HOW IT ADDRESSES THE SHOW CAUSE ORDER

        The ZGIA construct allows for generation to connect to the Transmission System without
injection rights, making it suitable to serve loads, including large loads, at the same substation.
This proposed construct not only formalizes the existing practice, but it also addresses a discrete
subset of the concerns identified by the Commission in the Show Cause Order, specifically those
concerning generator interconnection service and the study of generation serving co-located load.

         More specifically, the ZGIA construct provides a limited, structured option to support large
load integration through: (i) an interconnection service framework for generation that is supporting
co-located load; (ii) defined interconnection study processes tailored to zero-injection
configurations; (iii) potentially reduced network upgrade requirements where appropriate; and (iv)
clear allocation of operational and planning responsibilities. The ZGIA construct enables one
pathway for certain large load configurations to achieve speed to reliable power while maintaining
system reliability. The ZGIA framework is not, however, limited to large loads. While the ZGIA
is particularly responsive to the needs of a large load, a ZG Associated Load38 does not have to be
a large load.

         MISO notes that this filing does not include a proposed definition of “Large Load.” MISO
is continuing to refine the definition of “Large Load” through the ongoing stakeholder process at
the LLWG and expects to file the proposed definition of “Large Load” with the Commission in a
subsequent FPA section 205 filing that is responsive to certain additional concerns raised in the
Show Cause Order that are not specifically addressed herein. The ZGIA proposal remains just and
reasonable without inclusion of a definition of “Large Load” because the ZGIA proposal and the
identification of ZG Associated Load is open to application for all loads in the MISO region and
is not limited to only large loads. In addition, the Show Cause Order explains that it appears that
it would be reasonable to define a large load as: (1) a new commercial or industrial customer, (2)
located at a single site behind one or more points of interconnection, (3) that has a peak load of 50
MW or greater, (4) interconnects to the transmission system at a voltage level of greater than 69
kV, and (5) is not part of a co-location arrangement.39

         A.       The Rates, Terms, and Conditions of Service that Apply to Interconnection

        The Show Cause Order posits that MISO’s Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable
because it lacks provisions addressing with sufficient clarity and consistency the rates, terms, and
conditions of service that apply to interconnection customers serving co-located load.40 This filing
proposes to address the Show Cause Order’s concerns relating to the rates, terms, and conditions
of service that apply to interconnection customers serving co-located load as explained below:

        MISO proposes to implement a new type of service, called ZG Interconnection Service.
ZG Interconnection Service is service limited to serving specifically designated load that is either
at the same Point(s) of Interconnection (“POI”) or has a Point(s) of Withdrawal (“POW”) on the
same voltage side of the same substation as the ZGIA. ZG Interconnection Service is not
Transmission Service and does not exempt a Transmission Customer from procuring Transmission
Service. Accordingly, the ZGIA addresses the generator interconnection component of a co-
location arrangement; it does not establish or modify the Transmission Service that must be
obtained to serve the ZG Associated Load. MISO intends to address the separate transmission
service issues identified in the Show Cause Order through subsequent filings developed through
the LLWG.

        ZG Interconnection Service is fundamentally a limited product. ZG Interconnection
Service will be limited to a POI and POW that are at the same substation, with the same voltage
level. The ZGIA process will ultimately offer a ZGIA for limited operations, with operation limited
to ensure system reliability based upon the results of the impact assessment and facilities studies.
ZG Interconnection Service does not allow the Interconnection Customer to serve other load or
inject energy onto the Transmission System for purposes other than serving the ZG Associated
Load identified in the Interconnection Request and memorialized in the ZGIA. After engaging in
the stakeholder process, MISO determined that the same substation and voltage level limitation on
ZG Interconnection Service to only serve load or inject onto the Transmission System for purposes
of serving ZG Associated Load strikes the appropriate balance between offering a constrained
product that can be studied to ensure minimal impact on other projects and enabling an expedited
study process without hindering MISO’s ability to process the Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”).

       The rates, terms, and conditions for service under the ZGIA construct differ from ordinary
interconnection requests in several key areas listed below.

        First, the resource seeking ZG Interconnection Service must demonstrate a relationship
with load connected at the same voltage side of the same substation, defined as ZG Associated
Load, under which the ZG Associated Load signifies its intention to be served by the ZG Resource.
Mr. Keyser explains that, because ZG Interconnection Service allows the ZG Resource to serve
only its designated ZG Associated Load, documenting the relationship between ZG Associated
Load and the ZG Resource is necessary to prevent speculative Interconnection Requests from
using the process.41

respect to the Generating Facility and to the Transmission System is a critical component of ZG

         Transient Tolerance Window shall mean the period of time after a reduction or loss of
         load by the ZG Associated Load by the end of which window the Generating Facility
         with ZG Interconnection Service must have reduced its injections to an amount not
         greater than the Load of the ZG Associated Load. The Transient Tolerance Window shall
         be no greater than 20 seconds, and is further described by the Business Practices Manual
         for Large Load. The Transient Tolerance Window will be subject to Transmission Owner
         local planning criteria.

        Defining a “Transient Tolerance Window” is necessary to establish rules regarding how
quickly a Generating Facility must match ZG Associated Load reductions in Demand. As
explained further below and in the attached testimony of Mr. Keyser, even with tight coordination
between a Generating Facility and ZG Associated Load, a Generating Facility generally will not
be able to ramp down instantaneously in the event of a sudden decrease in Load.52 However, rules
are needed to require rapid disconnection or reduction in order to prevent impacts to the
Transmission System from unintended injections. The concept of a Transient Tolerance Window
therefore provides a reasonable vehicle for establishing realistic and enforceable rules about how
quickly a Generating Facility must reduce output.

        After careful consideration, MISO determined that a 20-second limit provides the best
system-wide balance between what is technically feasible and commercially practical on the one
hand, and minimizing even transient injections on the other hand. MISO notes that there may be
circumstances where a narrower window is necessary and practical given electrical topography on
certain parts of the MISO System, or Applicable Local Planning Criteria. It would be impractical
to identify all such circumstances in the Tariff. Therefore, the definition allows for the creation of
Business Practices Manual rules that narrow the window based on specific circumstances existing

        This service would provide a vehicle for a Generating Facility to serve a large load (or
other load) that is either located behind the same Point of Interconnection as the Generating
Facility as well as situations where the Point of Withdrawal of the load source is at the same
substation and voltage level as the Generating Facility. As Mr. Keyser explains in his testimony,
generators that are serving co-located load may not require the same degree of access to the
Transmission System as those seeking ERIS to serve Load farther afield. And the limited distance
over which energy would need to be—and is permitted to—flow allows for a more targeted study.55

        MISO worked closely with its stakeholders over many months, and prior to the issuance of
the Show Cause Order, to determine the appropriate permissible electrical distance between the
Generating Facility and load source that should be allowed for ZG Interconnection Service. As
part of this process, MISO initially considered allowing ZG Interconnection Service for a
Generating Facility to serve Load located several buses or substations away. However,
stakeholders across differing MISO sectors did not support such a broad reach, citing concerns
about the practicality of limiting injections to the rest of the Transmission System once the
generation and load were allowed to be at separate substations, the likelihood of unconstrained
power flows56 changing over time in unanticipated ways from what was studied, and the potential
for retail wheeling.

         MISO also considered limiting ZG Interconnection Service to load and generation located
behind the same Point of Interconnection. However, after discussions with stakeholders and
review of proposed configurations, MISO determined that such a restriction would be too narrow
for the MISO region. Several potential Interconnection Customers planned to utilize adjacent bays
in the same substation to run the lead lines for the Generating Facility and Load as a more
pragmatic and cost-effective approach than expanding one substation bay to house both lead lines
in order to maintain the same Point of Interconnection. These stakeholders argued that using an
adjacent bay would be electrically indistinguishable from housing both the Generating Facility and
Load behind the same bay given the requirement to install equipment limiting injections to the rest
of the Transmission System. Ultimately, MISO recognized that requiring the Generating Facility’s
Point of Interconnection and the Load’s Point of Withdrawal to be at the same voltage level of the
same substation provided the right balance of flexibility to enable expected large load co-location
arrangements while ensuring a minimal use of the Transmission System consistent with a
permanent zero injection based product. In reaching this decision, MISO noted that ‘same voltage
level at the same substation’ is the test applied for whether Points of Interconnection are electrically
identical under MISO’s Generating Facility Replacement Process. 57 Limiting the electrical

        MISO proposes new Section 1.11.1 to prohibit modifications to ZG Interconnection
Requests after submission. This prohibition is necessary and reasonable given the 90-day
timeframe for studies of Interconnection Requests for ZG Interconnection Service. To make this
timeframe workable and avoid delays that would impact other Interconnection Customers, it is
necessary to require that these Interconnection Services be well-considered and provide certainty
with respect to the details to be studied at the time they are submitted. This readiness requirement
is mitigated by the fact that MISO will study ZG Interconnection Requests on a quarterly basis.
Therefore, an Interconnection Customer that is not certain of the details to be included in its
Interconnection Request would only need to wait until the following quarter for another
opportunity to be studied.

        Section 3.11.1 includes one exception made necessary by process sequencing. MISO
proposes to require, and therefore allow, the ZG Interconnection Customer to move its Point of
Interconnection to the Transmission System if the ZG Associated Load subsequently moves the
Point of Withdrawal to not be at the same substation and voltage level as the Point of
Interconnection. In such circumstance, the Interconnection Customer would need to move its
proposed Point of Interconnection to match the move made by the ZG Associated Load. MISO
proposes to permit this move for several reasons. First, because the premise of ZG Interconnection
Service is based on the relative location of the ZG Associated Load and the ZG Resource, it is
more important from a system impact study perspective to prevent the Point of Interconnection
and Point of withdrawal from separating than it is to prevent the Point of Interconnection from
moving if the load’s location moves.77 Second, MISO expects that Interconnection Requests for
ZG Interconnection Service often will be submitted to MISO before transmission service is
requested by or on behalf of the ZG Associated Loads. This sequencing allows MISO to consider
the executed ZGIA in the transmission service study. Because the Interconnection Request for ZG
Interconnection Service likely will precede the transmission service study process, it is not
practical to hold the load to a proposed Point of Withdrawal before it has even submitted its own
application; doing so would undermine the scoping discussions between the load, its Load Serving
Entity, and the applicable Transmission Owner that occur during the load study process. This is
true under MISO’s current Tariff and business practices surrounding load integration studies and
MISO expects this sequencing to continue under other study processes currently being developed
to address the concerns raised in the Show Cause Order. MISO therefore submits that both the

               9. Section 3.11.2 Evaluation Process and Study Limits

        MISO proposes a quarterly study cadence for ZG Interconnection Service Interconnection
Requests as well as a limit of ten such Interconnection Requests per quarter. The quarterly cadence
aligns with the expected duration of the ZG Impact Assessment in order to avoid overlapping
studies. MISO determined that 10 such Interconnection Requests is an appropriate quarterly limit
because it balances opportunities for prompt study with avoiding the reduction of personnel and
resources needed to process the DPP, which will remain the primary focus of MISO’s
interconnection process. ZG Interconnection Service, while valuable, is a niche tool. MISO does
not expect to receive more than ten such Interconnection Requests a quarter as the process matures.
The proposed limit thus is a safeguard in case ZGIAs prove more popular than expected.

        In order to avoid undue disruption to the DPP, MISO proposes to allow Interconnection
Requests in the DPP to withdraw and commence the ZG Interconnection Service study process
only if they have not yet reached Decision Point II of their DPP cycle. This avoids the risk of
unscheduled restudy to other DPP Interconnection Requests because Interconnection Customers
currently can withdraw from the DPP at Decision Point II with such withdrawals being accounted
for in Phase 3 of the DPP. For the same reason, MISO does not propose to excuse withdrawing
Interconnection Requests from the currently-applicable penalty provisions of Section 7.6.2.1.1 and
7.8 of the DPP. The prohibition withdrawals after Decision Point II will be enforced through a one
year waiting period before an Interconnection Request for the same project can be processed for
ZG Interconnection Service. MISO believes that this is a sufficient deterrent against late stage
transfers.

requested stakeholder feedback on the proposed draft Tariff language.

        At the May 14, 2026 LLWG, MISO shared draft Tariff language reflecting the elements
ZGIA proposal relating to resource adequacy and markets and reliable operations. The draft Tariff
language incorporated stakeholder feedback regarding planning studies and multiple Points of
Injection. Specifically, in response to stakeholder feedback regarding MISO’s initial proposal
allowing multiple POIs, MISO proposed only allowing multiple POIs if the ZGIA is located at one
of the stations, i.e. Points of Withdrawal, of a Large Load Campus. MISO requested stakeholder
feedback on the draft Tariff language.

        At the May 27, 2026 PAC, MISO shared updated draft Tariff language with stakeholders
on the interconnection and planning elements of the ZGIA proposal. The draft Tariff language

93
     See Keyser, Attachment A – Table of Stakeholder Meetings.
 The Honorable Debbie-Anne Reese
August 18, 2026
Page 46


incorporated stakeholder feedback, including language specifying further detail of the ZGIA
interconnection studies, language clarifying that ZGIAs do not supersede state jurisdiction, and
revising the POI rules. MISO additionally decided not to pursue the campus approach in response
to stakeholder feedback. MISO requested stakeholder feedback on the proposed draft Tariff
language. At the June 10, 2026 LLWG, MISO reviewed the final ZGIA proposal with stakeholders
and provided draft Tariff language that incorporated stakeholder feedback. At the June 29, 2026
LLWG, MISO continued the dialogue regarding the ZGIA proposal to provide stakeholders an
opportunity to provide feedback on any remaining concerns and in response to the Show Cause
Order.

       At the July 15, 2026 PAC, MISO stated in its Liaison Report that the MISO Steering
Committee approved reassigning the ZIGA issue to the LLWG. The Liaison Report noted that it
received feedback in June on ZIGA Tariff redlines and that it posted a feedback response. For the
July 16, 2026 LLWG meeting, MISO posted ZGIA redlines for stakeholders to review. At the July
27, 2026 LLWG, MISO focused on other large load issues, but it provided a preliminary filing
timeframe that include the ZGIA filing. MISO discussed ZGIA at the August 12, 2026 LLWG and
provided updated Tariff redlines for stakeholders to review.

 V.      DOCUMENTS SUBMITTED IN THIS FILING

         In addition to this Transmittal Letter, this submission includes:

                  Tab A – Redline Tariff;94,95

                  Tab B – Clean Tariff;

                  Tab C – Prepared Direct Testimony of Marc Keyser; and

                  Tab D – Redline ZGIA to pro forma GIA (for informational purposes.



94
     Language currently pending before the Commission in the following, unrelated dockets is highlighted in yellow:
     Docket Nos. ER24-2046-003, ER26-2974-000, and ER26-3267-000. MISO requests that the Commission treat
     such highlighted language as subject to the outcomes of those pending proceedings. MISO commits to file any
     revisions to this highlighted language as necessary to comply with any Commission orders in those proceedings.
     In addition, MISO has not included language that has future effective dates of: 6/1/2027 in Docket No. ER26-
     1882-001, 6/12/2028 in Docket No. ER26-2825-000, 6/1/2029 in Docket No. ER22-1640-003, 9/1/2027 in
     Docket No. ER26-2974-000, 9/1/2027 in Docket No. ER25-1886-002 and 12/31/9998 in Docket No. ER26-1915-
     001. If needed, MISO commits to file any revisions to comply with any Commission orders in these proceedings
     and MISO commits to make subsequent filings with the Commission to reflect the most up-to-date version of the
     then-current Tariff provisions prior to the effective dates of the language.
95
     In this filing, MISO reconciled both the GIP (GIP Version 187) and ZGIA (GIA Version 111) to reflect the most
     current tariff language, which now incorporates provisions filed in compliance with FERC Order Nos. 2023 and
     2023-A. MISO requests that the Commission treat such pending language in Docket No. ER24-2406-003 as
     subject to the outcome of the pending proceeding. Additionally, MISO commits to submit any necessary revisions
     to the pending language to comply with any Commission orders in the proceeding.
  The Honorable Debbie-Anne Reese
 August 18, 2026
 Page 47


 VI.    EFFECTIVE DATE

         MISO requests an effective date of October 18, 2026 for the Tariff revisions submitted
 herein, which is not less than 60 days nor more than 120 days, after the filing date. This effective
 date will allow the revisions proposed herein to be effective expeditiously for stakeholders
 currently seeking a process to facilitate the types of co-location arrangements that this filing
 enables.

VII.    COMMUNICATIONS

         MISO respectfully requests waiver of Rule 203(b)(3) of the Commission’s Rules of

 commissions within the MISO Region and the Organization of MISO States. The filing has been
 posted electronically on MISO’s website at https://www.misoenergy.org/legal/ferc-filings/ for

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                       Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                     65.0.0, 66.0.0


   Facility: An electric generating unit or an electric generating station composed of one or more

          contiguous electric generating units aggregated at a single geographical site.

   Facilities Study: An engineering study conducted by the Transmission Provider or ITC in

          collaboration with the affected Transmission Owner(s) and ITC Participant(s) to

          determine the required modifications to the Transmission System, including the cost and

          scheduled completion date for such modifications, that will be required to provide the

          requested Transmission Service. The Transmission Provider shall have the final

          determination and ultimate responsibility for any such studies. Facilities Studies for any

          transmission facilities not under the operational control of the Transmission Provider

          shall be performed by the Transmission Owner, or ITC, or any entity it designates to

          perform the studies.

   Fast Ramping Resource: A Generation Resource that: (1) meets the qualification criteria of

          having a: (i) ramp rate greater than eighty (80) MW per minute; (ii) Fast Ramping

          Resource Performance Score that meets or exceeds the Fast Ramping Resource

          Performance Threshold when responding to regulation signals in Fast Ramping Resource

          Performance Tests; and (iii) duration greater than 20 minutes or more for Use Limited

          Resources; and (2) as such, will receive a fast changing regulation signal for a market

          interval for which it has been offered.

   Fast Ramping Resource Historical Performance Score: A performance score calculated on a

          Regulation Qualified Resource as the ratio of its Fast Ramping Resource Passed Intervals

          to its Fast Ramping Resource Valid Intervals in the Dispatch Intervals in all previous

          Hours when it was offered as a Fast Ramping Resource.




                                                                         Effective On: October 18, 2026
 MISO                                                                                                    1.F
FERC Electric Tariff                                                                        Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                      65.0.0, 66.0.0


   Fast Ramping Resource Passed Interval: An AGC signal interval, within a Fast Ramping

          Resource Performance Test, that is considered passed by a Resource offered as a Fast

          Ramping Resource for a particular Hour, during Regulating Reserve Deployment for the

          AGC signal interval if the MW response of the Resource for the Setpoint Instruction,

          adjusted for the communication delay, is within the tolerance range (i.e., +/- 0.25 MW if

          the delta change is 0.8 MW or less, and +/- 30 percent if the delta change is greater than

          0.8 MW).

   Fast Ramping Resource Performance Score: A score calculated during a Fast Ramping

          Resource Performance Test.

   Fast Ramping Resource Performance Test: A test performed in real time to evaluate the

          capability of a Regulation Qualified Resource that is offered as a Fast Ramping Resource

          to perform reliably as a Fast Ramping Resource while deploying Regulating Reserve.

          The test will be performed on such a Regulation Qualified Resource that is receiving

          either fast or regular regulation signals. At the start of each hourly interval, the Resource

          will be assigned an initial score that is the higher of the Fast Ramping Resource

          Historical Performance Score or the Fast Ramping Resource Performance Threshold.

          Within each hourly interval, at the end of each Dispatch Interval, a new adjustment to the

          initial score will be calculated as the ratio of Fast Ramping Resource Passed Intervals to

          Fast Ramping Resource Valid Intervals in the current and all previous Dispatch Intervals

          in the particular hourly interval.

   Fast Ramping Resource Performance Threshold: A minimum Fast Ramping Resource

          Performance Score of seventy percent (70%) that a Resource is required to meet to be




                                                                          Effective On: October 18, 2026
 MISO                                                                                                   1.F
FERC Electric Tariff                                                                       Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                     65.0.0, 66.0.0


          qualified as a Fast Ramping Resource.

   Fast Ramping Resource Valid Interval: An AGC signal interval is considered valid for a

          Resource undergoing a Fast Ramping Resource Performance Test, during its Regulating

          Reserve Deployment for an AGC signal interval, during which a new Setpoint Instruction

          is calculated that changes by a threshold MW of at least 0.1 MW from the previous

          Setpoint Instruction.

   Fast Start Resource: An online Generation Resource that is started, synchronized and injects

          Energy, or a Demand Response Resource that reduces its Energy consumption, within

          sixty (60) minutes of being notified and that has a minimum run time of one hour or less

          and that will participate in setting price as described in the process in Schedule 29A of

          this Tariff. A Fast Start Resource does not include fuel-limited resources such as pumped

          storage, Electric Storage Resources, run-of-river hydro, and wind resources. Offline

          Generation Resources will not participate in setting price as described in the process in

          Schedule 29A of this Tariff.

   Fast Start Resource All-In Energy Offer: The sum of an online Fast Start Resource’s Energy

          Offer, its amortized No Load Offer and, during its Minimum Run Time, its amortized

          Start up Offer; provided, that, in the case of a Demand Response Resource – Type I, it

          shall be the sum of the Energy Offer, its amortized Hourly Curtailment Offer and its

          amortized Shut-Down Offer over its minimum interruption duration.

   Fast Start Resource All-In Reference Level: The sum of an online Fast Start Resource’s

          Energy Reference Level, its amortized No Load Reference Level and, during its

          Minimum Run Time, its amortized Start up Reference Level; provided, that, in the case

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                      Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                    65.0.0, 66.0.0


          of a Demand Response Resource – Type I, it shall be the sum of the Energy Reference

          Level, its amortized Hourly Curtailment Offer Reference Level and its amortized Shut-

          Down Offer Reference Level over its minimum interruption duration.

   Feasibility Upgrade Process: The procedure that enables additional ARRs to be allocated based

          upon Network Upgrades as part of the MTEP process.

   Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Uniform System of Accounts: The

          Commission’s Uniform System of Accounts in the Code of Federal Regulations, Title 18,

          Conservation of Power and Water Resources, Parts 1-399, pursuant to which electric

          public utilities, licensees and other companies within FERC jurisdiction are required to

          maintain their books and records.

   Federal Power Marketing Agency: Any agency or instrumentality of the United States (other

          than the Tennessee Valley Authority), which sells electric Energy.

   FERC Market Rules: The market behavior rules and the prohibition against electricity Energy

          market manipulation codified by the Commission in its Rules and Regulations at 18 CFR

          § 1c.2 and 35.37, respectively; and any related proscriptions or any successor rules that

          the Commission from time to time may issue, approve or otherwise establish.

   File Transfer Protocol (FTP): The standardized File Transfer Protocol for data transfer.

   Final Planning Reserve Margin Requirement (Final PRMR): For LSEs not selecting the

          Reliability Based Demand Curve Opt Out, the PRMR established as a result of the PRA

          clearing using RBDCs. For LSEs selecting the RBDC Opt Out, Final PRMR is based on

          the sum of the applicable PRM plus the applicable RBDC Opt Out Adder. LSEs under

          state jurisdiction where the state has overridden the PRM established by the Transmission

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                     Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                   65.0.0, 66.0.0


          Provider will have a Final PRMR based on the planning reserve margin established by

          the state.

   Financial Schedule: A financial arrangement between two Market Participants designating a

          Source Point, Sink Point and Delivery Point establishing the obligations of the buyer and

          seller for the payment of Cost of Congestion and Cost of Losses. The Transmission

          Provider is not the Energy Market Counterparty to the sale of Energy under a Financial

          Schedule transaction and collects and disburses the Transmission Usage Charge as agent

          for the parties to the Financial Schedule.

   Financial Security: A Cash Deposit or Irrevocable Letter of Credit in an amount and form

          determined by and acceptable to Transmission Provider, provided by an Applicant and/or

          Tariff Customer to Transmission Provider as security.

   Financial Transmission Right (FTR): A financial instrument that entitles the holder to receive

          compensation for or requires the holder to pay certain congestion related transmission

          charges that arise when the Transmission System is congested and differences in

          Marginal Congestion Components of Day-Ahead Ex Post LMPs result.

   Firm Flow: The estimated impacts of firm transactions under network and point-to-point

          Transmission Service on a particular Coordinated Flowgate.

   Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service: Transmission Service under this Tariff that is

          reserved and/or scheduled between specified Points of Receipt and Points of Delivery

          pursuant to Module B of this Tariff.

   Firm Service Level: The MW portion of the total demand of a Demand Resource that is not

          subject to curtailment as a Demand Resource.

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                         Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                       65.0.0, 66.0.0


   First Planning Area: The Transmission System of the Transmission Provider Region as it

          existed immediately before the effective date of the Second Planning Area. The First

          Planning Area may be modified from time to time by: (1) the addition of any

          transmission facilities in the Midwest portion of the United States (i.e., Illinois, Indiana,

          Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, North Dakota, Ohio, South

          Dakota, and Wisconsin) where transmission facilities not under the functional control of

          the Transmission Provider are subsequently conveyed to the functional control of the

          Transmission Provider to be used to provide Transmission Service under Module B of the

          Tariff; or (2) the withdrawal from the Transmission Provider Region of a Member

          located in the First Planning Area.

   Fixed Carrying Charge: An annual charge calculated by taking the cost of service carrying

          charge elements expressed as a percent multiplied by the Transmission Owner or ITC’s

          rate base. The carrying charge elements include: operations and maintenance,

          depreciation expense, other taxes, return, and income taxes.

   Fixed Demand Bid: A request to purchase a specified MWh quantity of Energy, at specified

          locations in the Transmission Provider Region, during specific Hours of the next

          Operating Day submitted to the Day-Ahead Energy and Operating Reserve Market.

          Demand Bids may only be submitted by a Market Participant that is itself a Load Serving

          Entity (LSE) or is purchasing Energy to serve an LSE.

   Fixed Interchange Schedule: An Interchange Schedule consisting of a fixed, non-Dispatchable

          amount, used in the Energy and Operating Reserve Markets.

   Fixed Resource Adequacy Plan (FRAP): A plan submitted by an LSE through the MECT to

          the Transmission Provider that is approved by the Transmission Provider which

          demonstrates that the LSE has sufficient ZRCs to meet all or part of its Initial PRMR for

          one or more LRZs in a Season.

   Flowgate: A representative modeling of a facility or group of facilities that may act as a

          constraint to power transfer on the Bulk Electric System.

   Flowgate Rating: The Total Transfer Capability of a Flowgate.

   Forced Outage or Generator Forced Outage: An immediate reduction in output, Capacity or

          removal from service, in whole or in part, of a Generation Resource by reason of an

          Emergency or threatened Emergency, unanticipated failure, inability to return on

          schedule from a Planned Transmission Outage, or other cause beyond the control of the

          owner or operator of the facility, as specified in the relevant portions of the BPM for

          Outage Operations. A reduction in output or removal from service of a Generation

          Resource in response to changes in Energy Market conditions does not constitute a

          Generator Forced Outage.

   Forecast LSE Requirement: The forecasted Demand including the effect of all losses for an

          LSE at a CPNode for a Month less the Full Responsibility Purchases plus the Full

          Responsibility Sales and minus the Demand Resources that were registered to net for a

          given Month all at the same CPNode.

   Forecast Maximum Limit: For a Dispatchable Intermittent Resource, The the maximum MW

          level at which a Dispatchable Intermittentthe Resource is forecasted to operate. In

          addition, for a ZG Resource participating as a DIR, the maximum MW level at which a

          Resource may operate shall be less than the Demand of the Resource’s ZG Associated

          Loads.

   Foreign Guarantor: A Guarantor that is organized under the laws of a jurisdiction outside of

          the United States or Canada.

   Foreign Guaranty: A Corporate Guaranty accepted from a Guarantor that is organized under

          the laws of a jurisdiction outside of the United States or Canada.

   Forward Reliability Assessment Commitment (FRAC): A RAC process conducted up to seven

          (7) days prior to, and before the closing of, the Day-Ahead Energy and Operating

          Reserve Market.

   FTR and ARR Transactions Cleared But Not Yet Settled: This service category is a component

          of the FTR Potential Exposure. The FTR and ARR Transactions Cleared But Not Yet

          Settled are calculated on a monthly basis. If the net monthly value is positive, it is

          included in the FTR Potential Exposure calculation. If the net monthly value is negative,

          the value is not included in the FTR Potential Exposure calculation.

   FTR Auction: An auction conducted periodically through which the Transmission Provider,

          subject to the Simultaneous Feasibility Test: (i) awards FTRs of various durations and

          (ii) facilitates the selling of existing FTRs between Market Participants.

   FTR Auction Credit Allocation:        The amount of the Applicant’s and/or Tariff Customer’s

          Total Credit Limit allocated to FTR Auctions.

   FTR Auction Credit Exposure: Exposure to non-payment associated with the amount of the

          Applicant’s and/or Tariff Customer’s FTR Bids and Offers submitted in the auction.

   FTR Auction Participant: A Market Participant that participates in an FTR Auction

          administered by the Transmission Provider.

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                       Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                     65.0.0, 66.0.0


   FTR Auction Settled Transactions Exposure: The potential exposure to non-payment

          associated with FTR Auction transactions that have been cleared and settled.

   FTR Bid: A bid to purchase an FTR through an FTR Auction.

   FTR Bidder: A Market Participant submitting an FTR Bid.

   FTR Delivery Point: The transaction Delivery Point specified in a receipt point to delivery point

          FTR.

   FTR Holder: A Market Participant that owns one (1) or more FTRs.

   FTR MCP: The price at which a set of Comparable FTRs are sold through an FTR Auction.

   FTR Obligation: A receipt point to delivery point FTR that imposes a financial obligation on

          the FTR Holder if congestion exists in the direction from the FTR Delivery Point to the

          FTR Receipt Point.

   FTR Offer: An offer to sell an FTR through an FTR Auction.

   FTR Offeror: A Market Participant submitting an FTR Offer.

   FTR Option: A receipt point to delivery point FTR that imposes no financial obligations on the

          FTR Holder under any conditions.

   FTR Period: The period(s) of time on a given Day during which an FTR is in effect (On Peak,

          Off Peak, or full Day time period(s)).

   FTR Potential Exposure: The sum of exposure values as defined in Section V.B of Attachment

          L to this Tariff. Included are all FTR related charge types.

   FTR Potential Exposure Violation: A condition that exists whenever a Tariff Customer’s FTR

          Potential Exposure plus the larger of the FTR Auction Credit Allocation or FTR Auction

          Credit Exposure exceeds its Financial Security less its alternative capitalization

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                      Definitions - F

          requirement as further defined in Section V.C of Attachment L to this Tariff.

   FTR Quantity: The quantity in MW specified in an FTR.

   FTR Receipt Point: The transaction receipt point specified in an FTR.

   FTR Transactions Cleared But Not Yet Settled: The value of the FTRs based on the clearing

          price(s) established as a result of an FTR Auction which has been cleared, but has not yet

          been settled.

   Fuel Cost Uncertainty Adder: An amount determined by the Independent Market Monitor, not

          to exceed $100 per MWh, that is included in the Reference Level determination to

          account for fuel cost uncertainty when the resulting Reference Level exceeds $1,000 per

          MWh.

   Full Responsibility Purchases: The total of all purchases coincident with the expected Demand

          of the LSE under which the seller is contractually obligated to deliver Energy plus

          reserves to the purchaser, expressed in MWs for the hour. Reserve provision by the seller

          as a percent must meet or exceed the PRM obligation for the purchasing LSE. Up Ramp

          Capability and Down Ramp Capability by the seller as a percent must meet or exceed the

          PRM obligation for the purchasing LSE. Short-Term Reserve provision by the seller as a

          percent must meet or exceed the PRM obligation for the purchasing LSE. Each

          purchaser and seller must agree on which of their transactions are to be reported under

          this heading.

   Full Responsibility Sales: The total of all sales coincident with the expected Demand of the

          LSE under which the seller is contractually obligated to deliver Energy plus reserves to

          the purchaser, expressed in MWs for the hour. Reserve provision by the seller as a

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                      Definitions - F
MODULES                                                                                    65.0.0, 66.0.0


          percent must meet or exceed the PRM obligation for the purchasing LSE. Up Ramp

          Capability and Down Ramp Capability by the seller as a percent must meet or exceed the

          PRM obligation for the purchasing LSE. Short-Term Reserve provision by the seller as a

          percent must meet or exceed the PRM obligation for the purchasing LSE. Each

          purchaser and seller must agree on which of their transactions are to be reported.




                                                                         Effective On: October 18, 2026
 MISO                                                                                                 1.H
FERC Electric Tariff                                                                      Definitions - H
MODULES                                                                                    62.0.0, 63.0.0


   Headroom: For all Resources committed by the Transmission Provider in any real-time RAC

          processes or the LAC process conducted for the Operating Day, the difference between

          (i) the real-time Economic Maximum Dispatch and (ii) the sum of the Real-Time (a)

          Dispatch Target for Energy, (b) Dispatch Target for Regulating Reserve, (c) Dispatch

          Target for Spinning Reserve, (d) Dispatch Target for Supplemental Reserve, and (e)

          Dispatch Target for Short-Term Reserve.

   High Utilization Factor Unit (HUFU) Reserved Source Point (RSP): An RSP that does not

          qualify for inclusion in the BRSS per section 43.2.4.a.i.(b) but has a RSP Utilization

          Factor of seventy percent (70%) or greater.

   Historic Unit Consideration: A right to receive excess Planning Resource Auction revenue

          based on qualification described in Section 69A.7.7(a).

   Hour: A sixty (60) minute clock hour interval commencing the first second of each clock hour.

   Hot-to-Cold Time: The number of hours that must elapse between the time a Generation

          Resource, Demand Response Resource – Type II, or Electric Storage Resource is

          desynchronized and the time at which a cold Start-Up Offer would apply.

   Hot-to-Intermediate Time: The number of hours that must elapse between the time a

          Generation Resource, Demand Response Resource – Type II, or Electric Storage

          Resource is desynchronized and the time at which an intermediate Start-Up Offer would

          apply.

   Hourly Bi-Directional Ramp Rate: The MW/minute rate at which a Generation Resource, an

          External Asynchronous Resource, or Demand Response Resource - Type II can respond

          to either increasing or decreasing Setpoint Instructions that may be submitted to override




                                                                         Effective On: October 18, 2026
 MISO                                                                                                 1.H
FERC Electric Tariff                                                                      Definitions - H
MODULES                                                                                    62.0.0, 63.0.0


          the default value submitted during the asset registration process.

   Hourly Charge Ramp Rate: The MW/minute response rate for an Electric Storage Resource

          moving from zero output to its Hourly Economic Minimum Charge Limit and/or from the

          Hourly Economic Minimum Charge Limit to zero output that is utilized in the clearing of

          the Day-Ahead Energy and Operating Reserve Market and all Reliability Assessment

          Commitment processes, and in responding to either increasing or decreasing Setpoint

          Instructions between zero and the Hourly Economic Minimum Charge Limit that may be

          submitted to override the default value submitted during the asset registration process.

   Hourly Curtailment Offer: The compensation request, in dollars per Hour, in a Demand

          Response Resource-Type I Offer by a Market Participant representing the fees required

          for operating a Demand Response Resource Type I in an interrupted state.

   Hourly Discharge Ramp Rate: The MW/minute response rate for an Electric Storage Resource

          moving from zero output to its Hourly Economic Maximum Discharge Limit and/or from

          the Hourly Economic Maximum Discharge Limit to zero output that is utilized in the

          clearing of the Day-Ahead Energy and Operating Reserve Market and all Reliability

          Assessment Commitment processes, and in responding to either increasing or decreasing

          Setpoint Instructions between zero and the Hourly Economic Maximum Discharge Limit

          that may be submitted to override the default value submitted during the asset registration

          process.

   Hourly Economic Maximum Limit: The maximum MW level at which a Generation Resource,

          Demand Response Resource Type II, or External Asynchronous Resource may operate

          under normal system conditions that may be submitted to override the default value

FERC Electric Tariff                                                                      Definitions - H
MODULES                                                                                    62.0.0, 63.0.0


          submitted during the asset registration process. In addition, for a ZG Resource

          participating as a Generation Resource, the maximum MW level at which the Resource

          may operate under normal system conditions shall be less than the Demand of the

          Resource’s ZG Associated Loads.

   Hourly Economic Maximum Charge Limit: The maximum withdrawal MW level at which an

          Electric Storage Resource may operate under normal system conditions that may be

          submitted to override the default value submitted during the asset registration process.

   Hourly Economic Maximum Discharge Limit: The maximum injection MW level at which an

          Electric Storage Resource may operate under normal system conditions that may be

          submitted to override the default value submitted during the asset registration process. In

          addition, for a ZG Resource participating as an Electric Storage Resource, the maximum

          MW level at which the Resource may operate under normal system conditions shall be

   Hourly Economic Minimum Limit: The minimum MW level at which a Generation Resource,

          Demand Response Resource Type II, or External Asynchronous Resource may operate

   Calculation of Transmission Losses

   a.     The Transmission Provider shall calculate the LBA transmission loss percentages for

   each Season using the process described as follows:

          1.     The Transmission Provider's State Estimator calculates transmission losses (MW)

                 as part of the solution output process every five (5) minutes.

          2.     The transmission losses (MW) are computed on all transmission lines and

                 transformers by summing up real power at both ends for each transmission

                 element (retaining the convention for flow direction) or as the difference in real

                 power (without the sign convention for flow direction) for each State Estimator

                 solution.

          3.     The individual transmission losses (MW) for each element are summed to a total

                 transmission values for each Local Balancing Authorities (LBA) level.

          4.     These LBA transmission loss values are then integrated across each hour to

                 calculate an hourly transmission loss value (MW) for each LBA.

          5.     The total transmission loss value (MW) for each LBA will be the hourly

                 integrated transmission losses value (MW) for the hour of the Coincident Peak

                 Demand from the calendar year two years prior to the upcoming Planning Year.

          6.     For the purposes of the Transmission Provider Region, the LBA transmission loss

                 percentages are calculated as the total LBA transmission losses divided by the

                 total LBA peak data at that MISO peak hour for each Season. For purposes of a

                 Local Resource Zone, the LBA transmission loss percentages are calculated as the

                 total LBA transmission losses divided by the total LBA peak data at the LRZ peak

   Load Modifying Resources

   Load Modifying Resources can be offered as ZRCs in the PRA or can be used in FRAPs

   pursuant to Section 69A.9 or used in an RBDC Opt Out pursuant to Section 69A.9.1. As

   described below, a Demand Resource or a BTMG is eligible to qualify as a Load Modifying

   Resource if it meets the following requirements. A ZG Resource may qualify as a BTMG if not

   registered as a Generation Resource or DIR. All LMRs that are cleared in the PRA or were

   submitted in a FRAP for a Season or submitted in an RBDC Opt Out must be available for use in

   the event of an Emergency as declared by the Transmission Provider, pursuant to the Emergency

   operating procedures of the Transmission Provider, unless replaced with other ZRCs pursuant to

   Section 69A.3.1.h. ZRCs from Demand Resources will be grossed-up by the amount of avoided

   transmission losses in accordance with Section 68A.8.b and also by the applicable PRM in

   accordance with Section 68A.2. ZRCs from BTMGs will be grossed-up by the amount of

   avoided transmission losses in accordance with Section 68A.8.b. In accordance with the BPM

   for Resource Adequacy, the Transmission Provider will qualify an LMR for the applicable

   Season in the upcoming Planning Year. The amount of ZRCs from Demand Resources and

   BTMG has to be consistent with the expected reduction in demand at the time of the

   Transmission Provider’s expected Coincident Peak Demand.

   Majeure, or because the number of required deployments based on the registered number has

   been reached, the Market Participant representing the entity that had ZRCs from LMRs,

   including ZG Resources participating as BTMG, that cleared in the PRA, were used in a FRAP,

   or were used in an RBDC Opt Out will be subject to the following penalties in the event the

   LMR is called upon during an Emergency as declared by the Transmission Provider and the

   LMR fails to perform in accordance with its Market Participant’s response to such Market

   Participant’s Scheduling Instructions. The penalties defined below will only apply to the portion

   of the Market Participant’s response to such Market Participant’s Scheduling Instruction that is

   not followed during the Emergency declaration and will only be assessed by the Transmission

   Provider after giving the operator of the LMR an opportunity to provide documentation of the

   specific circumstances that would justify exemption from such penalties. There will not be an

   LMR penalty assessed for any portion of the Scheduling Instruction which had already been

   accomplished by an LMR for other reasons (e.g., for economic considerations, self-scheduling at

   or above the credited amount of BTMG or local reliability concerns in accordance with

   instructions from the Local Balancing Authority) at the time the request for interruption is made

   by the Transmission Provider. Likewise, for certain Demand Resources that are temperature

   dependent (e.g., a Demand Resource program involving air conditioning load), the specified

   Demand reduction may be adjusted in a manner defined in the measurement and verification

   procedures developed by the Transmission Provider to reflect the circumstances at the time a

   Demand Resource is called upon to reduce Demand.

   An LSE electing to use the RBDC Opt Out can continue to use its existing resource planning

   processes to meet its Final PRMR by providing the Transmission Provider with an RBDC Opt

   Out, as described below:

          a.     The RBDC Opt Out Lock-In Period will be three consecutive Planning Years for

                 all Seasons. If an LSE fails to submit an RBDC Opt Out then the LSE will be

                 required to participate in the PRA through any combination of the other Tariff-

            Seasonal Accredited Capacity (SAC) for a Capacity Resource that is a DRR or

   Generation Resource but not a Dispatchable Intermittent Resource, Intermittent Generation,

   Electric Storage Resource, External Resource, or Use Limited Resource will be determined

   described above, are here and after referred to as “Schedule 53 Resources”. A two-tiered

   during a Season and throughout the year. They include hours during Maximum Generation

   Emergency declarations and the hours when the operating margin, a measure of available supply

   capacity above demand and reserve requirements, is at its lowest.

   for each annual period (Annual RA Hours). Both Seasonal RA Hours and Annual RA Hours will

   be determined for the First Planning Area and Second Planning Area separately. The RA Hours

   determined in subpart III.A & III.B below are the only RA Hours that will be used to calculate

   Tier 2 ISAC in subpart V.C below. Where certain Seasonal RA Hours do not apply for a

                 Interconnection, (iii) an increase in the capacity of an Existing Generating

                 performed expeditiously depending on the specific information regarding any
                 proposed Generating Facility Modification and the existence of an Emergency
                 Condition.

   2.2    Comparability.
          Transmission Provider shall receive, process and analyze all Interconnection Requests in
          a timely manner as set forth in the GIP. Transmission Provider shall process and analyze
          Interconnection Requests from all Interconnection Customers comparably, regardless of
          Generating Facility ownership, and from all MHVDC Connection Customers
          comparably, regardless of MHVDC Transmission Line ownership.


   2.3    Base Case Data.
          Transmission Provider shall maintain base power flow, short circuit and stability
          databases, including all underlying assumptions, and contingency list on a password-
          protected website, subject to confidentiality provisions in GIP Section 13.1. In addition,
          Transmission Provider shall maintain network models and underlying assumptions on
          such password-protected website. Such network models and underlying assumptions
          should reasonably represent those used during the most recent Interconnection Study and
          be representative of current system conditions. A link to the information is provided on
          Transmission Provider’s OASIS site. Interconnection Customers and password-protected
          website users must sign a confidentiality agreement before the release of commercially
          sensitive information or Critical Energy Infrastructure Information in the Base Case data.
          Such databases and lists shall include all (i) generation projects and (ii) transmission
          projects, including merchant transmission projects that are proposed for the Transmission
          System for which a transmission expansion plan has been submitted and approved by the
          MISO Board.


   2.4    No Applicability to Transmission Service.
          Nothing in the GIP shall constitute a request for transmission service or confer upon an
          Interconnection Customer or MHVDC Connection Customer any right to receive
          transmission service or Wholesale Distribution Service under the Tariff.
