   Facility: An electric generating unit or an electric generating station composed of one or more

          contiguous electric generating units aggregated at a single geographical site.

   Facilities Study: An engineering study conducted by the Transmission Provider or ITC in

          collaboration with the affected Transmission Owner(s) and ITC Participant(s) to

          determine the required modifications to the Transmission System, including the cost and

          scheduled completion date for such modifications, that will be required to provide the

          requested Transmission Service. The Transmission Provider shall have the final

          determination and ultimate responsibility for any such studies. Facilities Studies for any

          transmission facilities not under the operational control of the Transmission Provider

          shall be performed by the Transmission Owner, or ITC, or any entity it designates to

          perform the studies.

   Fast Ramping Resource: A Generation Resource that: (1) meets the qualification criteria of

          having a: (i) ramp rate greater than eighty (80) MW per minute; (ii) Fast Ramping

          Resource Performance Score that meets or exceeds the Fast Ramping Resource

          Performance Threshold when responding to regulation signals in Fast Ramping Resource

          Performance Tests; and (iii) duration greater than 20 minutes or more for Use Limited

          Resources; and (2) as such, will receive a fast changing regulation signal for a market

          interval for which it has been offered.

   Fast Ramping Resource Historical Performance Score: A performance score calculated on a

          Regulation Qualified Resource as the ratio of its Fast Ramping Resource Passed Intervals

          to its Fast Ramping Resource Valid Intervals in the Dispatch Intervals in all previous

          Hours when it was offered as a Fast Ramping Resource.




                                                                         Effective On: October 18, 2026

MODULES                                                                                              66.0.0


   Fast Ramping Resource Passed Interval: An AGC signal interval, within a Fast Ramping

          Resource Performance Test, that is considered passed by a Resource offered as a Fast

          Ramping Resource for a particular Hour, during Regulating Reserve Deployment for the

          AGC signal interval if the MW response of the Resource for the Setpoint Instruction,

          adjusted for the communication delay, is within the tolerance range (i.e., +/- 0.25 MW if

          the delta change is 0.8 MW or less, and +/- 30 percent if the delta change is greater than

          0.8 MW).

   Fast Ramping Resource Performance Score: A score calculated during a Fast Ramping

          Resource Performance Test.

   Fast Ramping Resource Performance Test: A test performed in real time to evaluate the

          capability of a Regulation Qualified Resource that is offered as a Fast Ramping Resource

          to perform reliably as a Fast Ramping Resource while deploying Regulating Reserve.

          The test will be performed on such a Regulation Qualified Resource that is receiving

          either fast or regular regulation signals. At the start of each hourly interval, the Resource

          will be assigned an initial score that is the higher of the Fast Ramping Resource

          Historical Performance Score or the Fast Ramping Resource Performance Threshold.

          Within each hourly interval, at the end of each Dispatch Interval, a new adjustment to the

          initial score will be calculated as the ratio of Fast Ramping Resource Passed Intervals to

          Fast Ramping Resource Valid Intervals in the current and all previous Dispatch Intervals

          in the particular hourly interval.

   Fast Ramping Resource Performance Threshold: A minimum Fast Ramping Resource

          Performance Score of seventy percent (70%) that a Resource is required to meet to be

          qualified as a Fast Ramping Resource.

   Fast Ramping Resource Valid Interval: An AGC signal interval is considered valid for a

          Resource undergoing a Fast Ramping Resource Performance Test, during its Regulating

          Reserve Deployment for an AGC signal interval, during which a new Setpoint Instruction

          is calculated that changes by a threshold MW of at least 0.1 MW from the previous

          Setpoint Instruction.

   Fast Start Resource: An online Generation Resource that is started, synchronized and injects

          Energy, or a Demand Response Resource that reduces its Energy consumption, within

          sixty (60) minutes of being notified and that has a minimum run time of one hour or less

          and that will participate in setting price as described in the process in Schedule 29A of

          this Tariff. A Fast Start Resource does not include fuel-limited resources such as pumped

          storage, Electric Storage Resources, run-of-river hydro, and wind resources. Offline

          Generation Resources will not participate in setting price as described in the process in

          Schedule 29A of this Tariff.

          Offer, its amortized No Load Offer and, during its Minimum Run Time, its amortized

          shall be the sum of the Energy Offer, its amortized Hourly Curtailment Offer and its

          amortized Shut-Down Offer over its minimum interruption duration.

          Source Point, Sink Point and Delivery Point establishing the obligations of the buyer and

          seller for the payment of Cost of Congestion and Cost of Losses. The Transmission

          Provider is not the Energy Market Counterparty to the sale of Energy under a Financial

   Financial Transmission Right (FTR): A financial instrument that entitles the holder to receive

   First Planning Area: The Transmission System of the Transmission Provider Region as it

          existed immediately before the effective date of the Second Planning Area. The First

          Planning Area may be modified from time to time by: (1) the addition of any

          transmission facilities in the Midwest portion of the United States (i.e., Illinois, Indiana,

   Fixed Carrying Charge: An annual charge calculated by taking the cost of service carrying

          charge elements expressed as a percent multiplied by the Transmission Owner or ITC’s

          rate base. The carrying charge elements include: operations and maintenance,

          depreciation expense, other taxes, return, and income taxes.

   Fixed Demand Bid: A request to purchase a specified MWh quantity of Energy, at specified

          locations in the Transmission Provider Region, during specific Hours of the next

          Operating Day submitted to the Day-Ahead Energy and Operating Reserve Market.

          Demand Bids may only be submitted by a Market Participant that is itself a Load Serving

          Entity (LSE) or is purchasing Energy to serve an LSE.

   Flowgate: A representative modeling of a facility or group of facilities that may act as a

          constraint to power transfer on the Bulk Electric System.

   Flowgate Rating: The Total Transfer Capability of a Flowgate.

   Forced Outage or Generator Forced Outage: An immediate reduction in output, Capacity or

          removal from service, in whole or in part, of a Generation Resource by reason of an

          Emergency or threatened Emergency, unanticipated failure, inability to return on

          schedule from a Planned Transmission Outage, or other cause beyond the control of the

          owner or operator of the facility, as specified in the relevant portions of the BPM for

          Outage Operations. A reduction in output or removal from service of a Generation

          Generator Forced Outage.

   Forecast LSE Requirement: The forecasted Demand including the effect of all losses for an

          LSE at a CPNode for a Month less the Full Responsibility Purchases plus the Full

          Responsibility Sales and minus the Demand Resources that were registered to net for a

   Calculation of Transmission Losses

   a.     The Transmission Provider shall calculate the LBA transmission loss percentages for

   each Season using the process described as follows:

          1.     The Transmission Provider's State Estimator calculates transmission losses (MW)

                 as part of the solution output process every five (5) minutes.

          2.     The transmission losses (MW) are computed on all transmission lines and

                 transformers by summing up real power at both ends for each transmission

                 element (retaining the convention for flow direction) or as the difference in real

                 power (without the sign convention for flow direction) for each State Estimator

                 solution.

          3.     The individual transmission losses (MW) for each element are summed to a total

                 transmission values for each Local Balancing Authorities (LBA) level.

          4.     These LBA transmission loss values are then integrated across each hour to

                 calculate an hourly transmission loss value (MW) for each LBA.

          5.     The total transmission loss value (MW) for each LBA will be the hourly

                 integrated transmission losses value (MW) for the hour of the Coincident Peak

                 Demand from the calendar year two years prior to the upcoming Planning Year.

          6.     For the purposes of the Transmission Provider Region, the LBA transmission loss

                 percentages are calculated as the total LBA transmission losses divided by the

                 total LBA peak data at that MISO peak hour for each Season. For purposes of a

                 Local Resource Zone, the LBA transmission loss percentages are calculated as the

                 total LBA transmission losses divided by the total LBA peak data at the LRZ peak

          SECTION 2. SCOPE AND APPLICATION.


   2.1    Application of Generator Interconnection Procedures.
          a.     Sections 2 through 13 of the GIP apply to processing an Interconnection Request
                 pertaining to a Generating Facility. The GIP specifically applies when one of the
                 following is proposed by an Interconnection Customer: (i) a new Generating
                 Facility at a new Point of Interconnection that does not meet the criteria set forth
                 in Sections 2.1 (b) or (c), (ii) additional generation at an existing Point of
                 Interconnection, (iii) an increase in the capacity of an Existing Generating
                 Facility, (iv) a Generating Facility Modification that may constitute a Material
                 Modification to the operating characteristics of an Existing Generating Facility, or
                 (v) a Replacement Generating Facility. The evaluation in subpart (iv) will be
                 performed expeditiously depending on the specific information regarding any
                 proposed Generating Facility Modification and the existence of an Emergency
                 Condition.


          b.     Section 14 of the GIP applies to a request to interconnect a certified Small
                 Generating Facility meeting the certification criteria set forth in Appendix 3.


          c.     A request to interconnect a certified inverter-based Small Generating Facility no
                 larger than 10 kW shall be evaluated under the Appendix 4 – 10 kW Inverter
                 Process.


          d.     A request to interconnect to HVDC Facilities subject to Section 27A of the Tariff
                 will be incorporated into the queue as described in Sections 2 through 13 of the
                 GIP. Modifications to the process necessitated by the physics of a connection to
                 HVDC Facilities are found in Section 15 of the GIP, and will apply to those
                 requests to interconnect to HVDC Facilities.


          e.     Network Resource Interconnection Service is available to Existing Generating

   2.2    Comparability.

          Generating Facility ownership, and from all MHVDC Connection Customers
          comparably, regardless of MHVDC Transmission Line ownership.


   2.3    Base Case Data.
          Transmission Provider shall maintain base power flow, short circuit and stability
          databases, including all underlying assumptions, and contingency list on a password-
          protected website, subject to confidentiality provisions in GIP Section 13.1. In addition,
          Transmission Provider shall maintain network models and underlying assumptions on
          such password-protected website. Such network models and underlying assumptions
          should reasonably represent those used during the most recent Interconnection Study and
          be representative of current system conditions. A link to the information is provided on
          Transmission Provider’s OASIS site. Interconnection Customers and password-protected
          website users must sign a confidentiality agreement before the release of commercially
          sensitive information or Critical Energy Infrastructure Information in the Base Case data.
          Such databases and lists shall include all (i) generation projects and (ii) transmission
          projects, including merchant transmission projects that are proposed for the Transmission
          System for which a transmission expansion plan has been submitted and approved by the
          MISO Board.


   2.4    No Applicability to Transmission Service.
          Nothing in the GIP shall constitute a request for transmission service or confer upon an
          Interconnection Customer or MHVDC Connection Customer any right to receive

 1        I.     PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, BUSINESS ADDRESS, AND RELATIONSHIP TO

 3        THE MIDCONTINENT INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR, INC.

 4   A.   My name is Marc Keyser. I am the Director, Central Region—External Affairs for the

 5        Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”). My business address is 720

 6        City Center Drive, Carmel, IN 46032.

 7   Q.   PLEASE BRIEFLY DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL

 8        BACKGROUND.

 9   A.   I hold a Bachelor of Science and Engineering Degree in Nuclear Engineering, a Bachelor

10        of Science and Engineering Degree in Engineering Physics, and a Master of Science and

11        Engineering Degree in Nuclear Engineering – Plasma Physics. I have been employed by

12        MISO since February, 2007 in a variety of different roles. I spent six years in a market

13        design and market / operational engineering role. As MISO worked to launch its Energy

14        and Ancillary Services Markets, I led the design of the Automatic Generation Control

15        System. Since that time, I have held leadership roles in Client and Stakeholder Relations,

16        Corporate Strategy, and Program Management. Prior to joining MISO, I worked from

17        2002-2007 in various system operation roles for Consumers Energy, an investor-owned

18        utility in Michigan.

19   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR CURRENT ROLE AND RESPONSIBILITIES.

20   A.   In my current role, I provide advisory services across MISO business areas and manage

21        relationships with key MISO stakeholders across the central region of the MISO footprint.

22        Given my length and breadth of experience, I was chosen to act as the MISO liaison to the

23        newly-formed Large Load Working Group (“LLWG”) in March 2026. As the LLWG
                                                                                        Tab C
                                                                                        Page 2

 1        liaison, I coordinate MISO’s planned activities with respect to our large load stakeholder

 2        efforts. Since October 2025, I have also led MISO’s effort to create and formalize the

 3        proposal accompanying my testimony. As part of this responsibility, I have closely

 4        examined existing and proposed co-location arrangements in the MISO region and the rule

 5        sets that govern them.

 6   Q.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY SUBMITTED TESTIMONY IN A REGULATORY

 7        PROCEEDING?

 8   A.   No. This is the first testimony that I have provided in any regulatory proceeding.

 9                              II.     PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY

10   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

11   A.   My testimony supports two related items. First, my testimony supports the proposed Tariff

12        revisions submitted in this docket to implement Zero Injection Generator Interconnection

18   A.   Fundamentally, HILLGA and ZG Interconnection Service serve the same goal: allowing

19        for the rapid study and development of generation needed on an accelerated basis to serve

20        a specific load need. Both constructs balance a need for rapid study with protection of the

21        Transmission System and avoidance of negative impacts to other Interconnection

22        Customers. Both also rely on proximity of the generation to the load to minimize impacts

23        to the broader system.     In minimizing the potential for unexpected impacts to the
                                                                                         Tab C
                                                                                       Page 20

 1        Transmission System, there are two design considerations that can be scoped in relation to

 2        each other to achieve balance: (1) duration of service, and (2) narrowness of design scope.

 3        The more of the transmission system that is allowed to be used (i.e., the permitted electrical

 4        remoteness of the generation and load), the greater the potential for impacts to the system

 5        to change in unexpected ways. This is because it becomes harder to truly isolate injections.

 6        The main protections against system impacts thus are reliable modelling and the

 7        consistency of the generation and load to the modelling assumptions. This is more of a

 8        short-term focused solution. The longer that service is allowed to remain, the more it

 9        provides upfront cost certainty to Interconnection Customers. But the tradeoff is that the

10        system will change over time and impact assumptions may change with it. Shorter term

11        service like SPP’s HILLGA allows for impacts to be mitigated or made temporary because

12        the service will be replaced with something permanent after only a few years. A permanent

13        product, like ZG Interconnection Service relies on tight geographical requirements (i.e.,

14        co-location of the ZG Resource and ZG Associated Load at the same substation) and

15        isolation from the rest of the Transmission System (i.e. prevention of injection) to ensure

16        that even if the Transmission System changes over the course of decades, the impact of the

17        ZG Resource will remain similar to the initial impacts modeled as part of the ZGIA study

18        process.

19   Q.   WHY IS MISO PROPOSING THE ZGIA CONSTRUCT AS A PERMANENT

20        PRODUCT INSTEAD OF A SHORTER-TERM PRODUCT?

21   A.   MISO selected the ZGIA approach to promote an efficient interconnection process and

22        accelerate service to load, while also preserving equitable treatment of interconnection

23        customers and accommodating preexisting arrangements. Stated differently, the ZGIA
                                                                                      Tab C
                                                                                     Page 21

 1        framework balances the requirement that generators injecting onto the Transmission

 2        System be studied and appropriately mitigated with the recognition that certain on-site

 3        generation serves local load without exporting power to the broader Transmission System.

 4        The ZGIA approach builds from experience in the MISO footprint and recognizes both

 5        stakeholder preferences and the types of co-location and near co-location configurations

 6        that MISO has encountered and expects to see in the future.

 7   Q.   WHY IS IT IMPORTANT TO HAVE A GIA FOR A GENERATOR THAT DOES

 8        NOT PLAN TO INJECT ENERGY ONTO THE TRANSMISSION SYSTEM?

 9   A.   Historically, MISO has only rarely encountered Interconnection Customers seeking to

10        connect to the Transmission System without injecting energy. However, with the advent

11        of significant large load additions, MISO has seen these types of arrangements become

12        more common and expects this trend to continue. Therefore, it is now important to

13        implement a service type and study process that specifically recognizes both the challenges

14        and opportunities associated with large loads, leverages the increased commercial

15        attractiveness of pairing generation with a specific nearby load, and tailors an

16        Interconnection Service study process to their needs. The proposed ZG Interconnection

17        Service and ZGIA framework provide a critical first step to better enabling large loads

18        while also maintaining equitable interconnection principles–resource injections on the grid

19        must be studied, and their impacts to prior-queued and operational resources must be

20        mitigated, and other Interconnection Requests should not be harmed.

21               If a Generating Facility is connected to MISO’s Transmission System and has the

22        ability to inject energy onto the Transmission System, MISO must have visibility into how

 4   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE ZG INTERCONNECTION SERVICE.

 5   A.   ZG Interconnection Service is service limited to serving specifically designated load that

 6        is either at the same Point of Interconnection (“POI”) or has a Point of Withdrawal

 7        (“POW”) on the same voltage side of the same substation as the ZGIA. Like other forms

 8        of Interconnection Service in MISO, ZG Interconnection Service is not Transmission

 9        Service and does not exempt a transmission customer, including a transmission customer

10        serving a large load, from procuring Transmission Service.

11   Q.   WHAT IS A POINT OF WITHDRAWAL AND HOW DOES IT RELATE TO THE

12        ZGIA?

13   A.   A Point of Withdrawal is a newly-defined term that describes the point that a Load

14        interconnects to the Transmission System. It is the Load analog to the generation-specific

15        term “Point of Interconnection”. It is important that this connection point is specified with

16        respect to ZG Interconnection Service, because resources are limited to taking ZG

17        Interconnection Service only at the same substation and voltage level of the Point(s) of

18        Withdrawal of their ZG Associated Load.

20        PRODUCT.

21   A.   As noted below, ZG Interconnection Service allows the Interconnection Customer to

22        connect at the substation and voltage level of its ZG Associated Load. ZG Interconnection

23        Service does not allow the Interconnection Customer to serve other load or inject energy

 2        Associated Load identified in the Interconnection Request and memorialized in the ZGIA.

 4        Service are robust, including obligations to implement equipment and/or operational

 5        procedures to prevent injections onto the Transmission System beyond the substation

 7   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE WHY MISO IS UTILIZING A TRANSIENT TOLERANCE

 8        WINDOW?

 9   A.   The Transient Tolerance Window is a requirement for the ZG Resource to disconnect or

10        reduce output if the ZG Associated Load trips or has a significant load reduction. In this

11        event, if the same breaker does not supply both the ZG Resource and the ZG Associated

12        Load, the Resource will not automatically disconnect along with the ZG Associated Load.

13        Therefore it is not realistic to prohibit all transient injections. Some time period must be

14        allowed for the generator to ramp down or disconnect to match the demand of the ZG

15        Associated load. During this time, incidental flows onto the Transmission System can

16        occur. The Transient Tolerance Window provides a required time frame for the ZG

17        Resource to disconnect or match ZG Associated Load demand.

18   Q.   WHY DID MISO CHOOSE 20 SECONDS AS THE TRANSIENT TOLERANCE

19        WINDOW?

20   A.   The Transient Tolerance Window is limited to values less than or equal to 20 seconds in

21        order to align with the MTEP modeling interval of 20 seconds for transient stability

22        analysis. This ensures that a generator will be robustly evaluated for stability impacts to

23        ensure that it will operate without unnecessary tripping for momentary conditions that do
                                                                                      Tab C

 2        further limit the Transient Tolerance Window to values less than 20 seconds.

 3   A.   ZG Resources will be accredited like any other Capacity Resource of the appropriate

 4        technology type except that a ZG Resource will offset no more than the coincident peak

 5        demand of the ZG Associated Load, plus an accounting for system losses not experienced

 6        due to the co-location of load and generation. ZG Resources will not be able to offset any

 7        other loads, because the ZG Resource is not able to inject onto the Transmission System.

 8   Q.   IS A ZG RESOURCE THAT PARTICIPATES IN MISO’S RESOURCE

 9        ADEQUACY CONSTRUCT SUBJECT TO A MUST OFFER REQUIREMENT?

10   A.   Yes. As a Capacity Resource, a ZG Resource will be subject to the “must offer” obligation

11        into the MISO’s Day-Ahead Energy Markets when it clears the PRA, with the exception

12        that the must-offer obligation is limited to the expected demand of the ZG Associated Load

13        for the next Operating Day.

14   Q.   HOW IS A ZG RESOURCE ABLE TO PARTICIPATE IN MISO’S RESOURCE

15        ADEQUACY CONSTRUCT?

16   A.   To ensure that the limitations of the ZG Resource are respected, and to prevent the potential

17        for ZRC sales from a ZG Resource to a load other than the ZG Associated Load, ZGIA

18        Resources must be in a Fixed Resource Adequacy Plan (“FRAP”) or RBDC Opt-Out of

19        the Market Participant that has the Planning Reserve Margin Requirement of the ZG

20        Associated Load. Further, ZG Resource are not eligible to replace ZRCs throughout the

21        Planning Year.

22               VI.       ZG RESOURCE PARTICIPATION IN THE ENERGY

23                          AND OPERATING RESERVE MARKETS
                                                                                       Tab C
                                                                                      Page 38

 1   Q.   ARE ZGIA RESOURCES REQUIRED TO REGISTER AND PARTICIPATE IN

 2        MISO MARKETS?

 3   A.   ZGIA Resources that are greater in size than 5 MW will be required to register and

 4        participate as either Generation Resources, Dispatchable Intermittent Resources, or Energy

 5        Storage Resources in the MISO Energy and Ancillary Service Markets. This requirement

 6        ensures that ZG Resources and their ZG Associated Loads are allocated a share of market-

 7        distributed costs in proportion to the benefits received. Certain market charges such as the

 8        provision of ancillary services for load, and administrative charges, are billed based on

 9        gross MW volumes in the Day-Ahead and Real-Time markets. By requiring ZGIA

10        Resources to register as market resources, MW volumes for both load and generation will

11        be captured separately, resulting in appropriate billing of these charges under already-

12        applicable Tariff rules for market settlements.

13   Q.   WHY ARE ALL ZGIA RESOURCES NOT REQUIRED TO REGISTER AND

14        PARTICIPATE IN MISO MARKETS?

15   A.   MISO proposes not to require any ZG Resource smaller than 5 MW in size to register and

16        participate as a market resource, because this is the de minimis size threshold that MISO

17        typically provides for Resource registration.

18   Q.   HOW WILL A ZG RESOURCE MAINTAIN ITS OUTPUT BELOW THE

19        CONSUMPTION OF THE ZG ASSOCIATED LOAD WHILE RESPONDING TO

20        DISPATCH INSTRUCTIONS FROM MISO?

21   A.   MISO’s Day-Ahead and Real-Time markets create economically efficient dispatches to

22        generators that account for the physical and economic capabilities of resources. ZG

23        Resources are required to submit maximum limit offers that are at most equal to the demand
                                                                                        Tab C
                                                                                      Page 39

 1        expectation of the ZG Associated Load. With this requirement, the Offers of a ZG Resource

 2        will have to be updated throughout the Operating Day. With this maximum limit in place,

 3        the dispatch instruction from MISO will be less than or equal to the offsetting demand of

 4        the ZG Associated Load, with no resulting injections.

 5   Q.   CAN A ZG RESOURCE QUALIFY TO PROVIDE OPERATING RESERVES?

 6   A.   Yes. A ZGIA Resource that meets the eligibility requirements can provide operating

 7        reserves. Operating Reserves are cleared when energy dispatches of a resource are between

 8        its maximum and minimum limits, and Operating Reserve deployments do not result in

 9        resource setpoint instructions exceeding the maximum limit. By requiring a maximum

10        limit that is less than the demand expectation of the ZG Associated Load, operating reserve

11        deployments will not result in injections. Again, the Offers of a ZGIA Resource will have

12        to be updated throughout the Operating Day to reflect the expected demand of the ZG

13        Associated Load

14   Q.   WILL ZG RESOURCES BE ELIGIBLE TO PROVIDE REACTIVE POWER?

15   A.   Yes. Reactive power does not perform the useful work of the power grid; instead, it

16        supports the system voltage and magnetic fields necessary for reliable operation of the grid.

17        The need for reactive power varies by location and system conditions. Because the

18        provision of reactive power is distinctive from the injection of real power, ZG Resources

19        will be eligible to provide reactive power.
